title: Intense Asymmetry and Self-Flagellation: why comparing your business to others is irrational
summary: Jason Cohen uses Erica Douglass's self-doubt after selling her company for $1M to show why driven founders torment themselves with comparisons. Businesses are asymmetrical in time, market, team, location and everything else, so comparing yours to another is comparing the incomparable.

principles.text: No two businesses are symmetrical, so comparing your results to another company's is irrational.
principles.quote: Well it's obvious where two businesses are symmetrical: Nowhere!

principles.text: Businesses differ in time, location, market, team, features, investors and followers; you can't predict success from apparent similarity.
principles.quote: In fact they're asymmetrical in everything--location, the market they serve, the features they have, the founding team, their natural talents and gaps, the investors (if any), the amount of money raised (if any), the number of social media followers and everything else.

principles.text: Use apparent similarity to a competitor only as a spark for ideas (like a marketing tactic), not as a yardstick for yourself.
principles.quote: It's healthy to use (apparent) symmetry to spark an idea, e.g. "That's a creative marketing campaign, maybe we could try something similar."

principles.text: Analogy pitches like "Netflix for X" imply a symmetry that doesn't hold; each company has new variables and is unpredictable.
principles.quote: each company is a new challenge, with new variables, and unpredictable.

principles.text: Driven people self-select the metrics that make them feel inadequate; the stated reason is a rationalization, not the cause.
principles.quote: In fact, you could credibly argue that she's intentionally selecting only those elements which will cause her to feel inadequate, ignoring those to the contrary.

principles.text: Stop comparing yourself to something that is objectively incomparable.
principles.quote: Stop comparing yourself to something that is objectively incomparable.
